sections.learningObjectives:
- Describe the four parts of Medicare (A, B, C, and D), including the types of services each covers and basic eligibility concepts.
- Describe Medicaid as a joint federal-state program, including how eligibility and benefits can vary by state.
- Compare and contrast Medicare and Medicaid, including administration, funding, and eligible populations.
- Recognize key billing implications for the medical office assistant, including eligibility verification, coordination of benefits, ABNs, and payer order for dual-eligible patients.
- Apply scope-of-practice boundaries by gathering and routing information and escalating coverage, enrollment, and payment questions to clinicians and billing professionals.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Medicare is like a big club card from the national government that helps older people and some sick younger people pay for doctor and hospital care.

### Question 2

CMS is the office that keeps the Medicare club running; the Social Security office helps people sign up, but CMS is in charge.

### Question 3

Think of Medicare like a birthday present from the government that most people can open when they turn 65.

### Question 4

Medicare isn't only for older grown-ups; some younger people who are very sick or who have a serious kidney problem can join too.

### Question 5

If someone's kidneys stop working and they need dialysis, Medicare can help pay no matter how old they are.

### Question 6

Part A is paid for like a piggy bank people fill up with a little money from every paycheck while they work.

### Question 7

Part A is the 'hospital' part of Medicare; it helps pay when someone has to stay overnight in the hospital.

### Question 8

Part A also helps pay for special rehab and nursing care in a skilled facility after a hospital stay, but not for permanent help with everyday tasks.

### Question 9

If you (or your spouse) paid into the system through work for about ten years, Part A is free like a prepaid membership.

### Question 10

Part B is the 'doctor visit' part; it helps pay when you see a doctor or get care without staying overnight in the hospital.

### Question 11

People who earn more money pay a little extra each month for Part B, like paying a higher ticket price for a nicer seat.

### Question 12

For most doctor visits, Medicare pays 80 cents of every covered dollar and the patient pays the other 20 cents.

### Question 13

Part B helps pay for things like checkups to catch problems early and equipment like walkers and wheelchairs.

### Question 14

Part B is like an optional add-on to your membership; if you wait too long to add it, you may pay a little extra each month.

### Question 15

Original Medicare is the basic two-part package: Part A for the hospital and Part B for the doctor.

### Question 16

Going to see the doctor without staying overnight is a Part B thing, like a regular checkup visit.

### Question 17

Medicare can help pay for nurses or therapists who come to your house when you are too sick to easily go out for care.

### Question 18

Part A helps pay for comfort care at the end of life when someone chooses hospice instead of more hospital treatment.

### Question 19

A 'benefit period' is like a fresh start each time you are admitted to the hospital after being out for a while, and a new deductible can apply.

### Question 20

If the service costs $100 and the deductible is already paid, the patient pays $20 and Medicare pays the other $80.

### Question 21

Medicare mostly does not pay for regular teeth cleanings or false teeth, which surprises many people.

### Question 22

It's like checking that a coupon is still valid before you go to the store, so there are no surprises at the cash register.

### Question 23

Medicare now uses a special code made of letters and numbers instead of your Social Security number, to keep your private number safer.

### Question 24

The MBI is a steady ID code like a locker number; it stays the same and hides your Social Security number.

### Question 25

The CMS-1500 form is like the checkout slip a doctor's office sends to Medicare to ask for payment for a visit.

### Question 26

Medicare hires special helper companies, called MACs, to read each bill and decide how much Medicare should pay.

### Question 27

Accepting assignment is like agreeing to the store's set price and promising not to add extra hidden charges.

### Question 28

A doctor who signs up to fully work with Medicare promises not to surprise the patient with extra bills on covered care.

### Question 29

An ABN is like a 'heads up' note telling the patient, 'Medicare might not pay for this, and if not, you may have to.'

### Question 30

If a working older person has big-company job insurance, that job insurance usually pays first and Medicare pays second, like a backup.

### Question 31

Part C is like choosing a private 'bundled' plan instead of the basic government package.

### Question 32

Medicare lets private insurance companies run special plans as long as Medicare approves them and watches over them.

### Question 33

A Part C plan must give you at least everything Parts A and B would, and it might throw in extras like drug coverage.

### Question 34

With these plans, you usually have to visit doctors who are 'on the team list,' or you may pay more.

### Question 35

Even if you pick a private Part C plan, you still keep paying the regular Part B 'doctor coverage' fee each month.

### Question 36

Part D is the 'medicine' part of Medicare that helps pay for drugs you pick up at the pharmacy.

### Question 37

Part D is an optional 'medicine club' you join separately through a private company.

### Question 38

The formulary is like a menu of medicines the plan will help pay for, with some items costing more than others.

### Question 39

Waiting too long to join the medicine plan without other good drug coverage means paying a little extra every month as a penalty.

### Question 40

Medigap is like a helper that pays the leftover coins and deductibles after Original Medicare pays its share.

### Question 41

Medigap only works with the basic government Medicare, not with a private Part C plan—you can't use the helper with the wrong membership.

### Question 42

Private insurance companies are the shops that sell the 'gap-filler' Medigap plans.

### Question 43

The MSN is like a receipt report that arrives every few months showing what Medicare paid for and what the patient might still owe.

### Question 44

The NPI is like a doctor's official ID badge number that goes on every bill so Medicare knows who gave the care.

### Question 45

The doctor is not allowed to ask the patient to pay the 'extra' amount Medicare didn't cover beyond the usual share.

### Question 46

Coordination of benefits is like figuring out which parent pays first when two grown-ups share the cost of a school trip.

### Question 47

A dual eligible is someone who holds two different 'assistance cards' at once—Medicare and Medicaid working together.

### Question 48

For patients with both cards, Medicare pays first and then passes the leftover part to Medicaid, like a relay race.

### Question 49

Medicaid is a helping-hand program where the national government and each state chip in together to help people with lower incomes get care.

### Question 50

Each state runs its own version of Medicaid, a bit like each classroom following the same school rules but with its own teacher.

### Question 51

Medicaid mostly looks at whether a person or family's income is low enough to need help, along with a few other rules.

### Question 52

Medicaid helps many different kinds of people—kids, moms-to-be, older people, and people with disabilities—when they need a hand.

### Question 53

CHIP is a special program to help kids whose families earn a little too much for Medicaid but still can't afford private insurance.

### Question 54

Medicaid waits its turn; if there is other insurance, that insurance pays first, and Medicaid helps with what is left.

### Question 55

To get paid by Medicaid, a doctor has to sign up with that state's Medicaid office, like registering at each separate library system.

### Question 56

Some states chose to let more low-income grown-ups join Medicaid, with the national government helping pay for it.

### Question 57

QMB is like a kind friend who helps pay your Medicare bills—the monthly fee and the leftover costs—if your income is low.

### Question 58

Medicaid cards can expire or change, so the office checks with the state each time, like confirming a ticket is still valid before a show.

### Question 59

Sometimes a state hires private companies to help run Medicaid, like hiring a coach to organize a big sports team.

### Question 60

Medicare is the age-and-disability club run by the nation; Medicaid is the income-based helping hand shared by the nation and each state.

### Question 61

Copy everything important from both sides of the card, like writing down a friend's full name, membership number, and the dates it works.

### Question 62

You can't let the customer pick which card gets charged first; there are rules about which insurance goes first.

### Question 63

Collecting the patient's fair share at the desk is like paying your part of a shared dinner bill when it arrives.

### Question 64

The office hands the patient a 'just so you know' note before doing something Medicare might not pay for, so there are no surprise bills.

### Question 65

Don't make promises you can't keep; pass the tricky question to the grown-up expert who checks coverage.

### Question 66

With Medicaid, the office usually can't ask the patient to pay the leftover part of the bill, except tiny allowed copays for some people.

### Question 67

When someone's membership card changes, update the notebook right away so bills go to the right place.

### Question 68

A ticket can expire or change, so the office checks it every time before the show starts.

### Question 69

If the card looks old, don't guess—check with the state's system to see if coverage is really still active.

### Question 70

Usually Medicare goes first and the old-job plan helps second, but the office should always double-check the rules for that exact plan.

### Question 71

Medicare pays for a special 'check-in' visit called the Annual Wellness Visit, but not the big head-to-toe physical many people think of.

### Question 72

Bills have a 'turn in by this date' rule; if you turn them in too late, they won't be paid.

### Question 73

A clean bill has all the important facts filled in correctly, like a homework page with every blank answered.

### Question 74

The assistant helps gather the paperwork for 'permission first,' but the doctor and the insurance company make the actual decisions.

### Question 75

If you see someone doing something dishonest, tell the right grown-up in charge so it can be fixed, instead of looking away.

### Question 76

There is a special sign-up window around your 65th birthday, like the first few days you can join a club.

### Question 77

People with higher incomes pay a little extra on their Medicare medicine and doctor premiums, like a slightly higher club fee.

### Question 78

Each state runs its own version of the helping-hand program, so the rules can be different depending on where you live.

### Question 79

Medicare goes first in the relay, and Medicaid picks up the leftover parts afterward.

### Question 80

Ask the official system for the real, up-to-date answer instead of guessing from what someone remembers.

### Question 81

If the workplace is a small company, Medicare usually pays first, like being the first person to chip in.

### Question 82

If the patient signed the 'you might have to pay' note before the service, then when Medicare says no, the patient may owe the bill.

### Question 83

A tiny copay shouldn't stop someone from getting the care they need; the office follows the rules and doesn't turn people away over it.

### Question 84

Original Medicare is the government's basic plan; Part C is a private company's plan that must at least match the basics.

### Question 85

In the medicine plan, there is a middle stage where your share of drug costs changes for a while before the plan kicks back in more.

### Question 86

Gently explain that these are two different helping programs, and some people actually get both at the same time.

### Question 87

Choosing a plan is a big decision, so the office points people to a neutral helper who is trained to explain the options.

### Question 88

The Medicare card is like a membership card with your name, your member number, and the date your membership starts.

### Question 89

The office asks how you qualified—birthday, disability, or kidney condition—because it can change a few coverage details.

### Question 90

When the office gets the insurance details right, bills get paid on time and patients aren't surprised—like filling out a form perfectly so there are no problems.
